edits.quote: Shapes are actual size: each small triangle side is 1 inch. Print at 100%.   This bar is 1 inch: (and 'Boards are actual size...' on pp. 2-5)
edits.fix: Replace the print note with the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / PGQUG-K1' on every page; put the print-at-100% check in the adult notes (wording also inconsistent: 'Shapes' vs 'Boards').

edits.quote: 1  How many greens?
edits.fix: Delete the title; label 'Problem 1:'.
Delete the Name field.

edits.quote: Four outlines that are exactly single blocks: blue rhombus, red trapezoid, yellow hexagon, purple chevron (answers 2, 3, 6, 4)
edits.fix: Each outline is one block, so a child can lay the block on it and the count is immediate; this repeats free play and is the 'dumbed down' K-1 opener he complains about. Replace with composite outlines that need 6-12 greens and can be filled several ways, or fold the counting into P4.

edits.quote: Cover it all up!
edits.fix: Delete; 'Put green triangles on each shape' already says it.

edits.quote: Talk about it. Which shape needs the most greens? Which needs the fewest? Can you cover the yellow shape with blue blocks instead?
edits.fix: Move the comparison questions to the adult notes; if the blue-cover task is wanted, state it in the problem with a box for the number of blues.

edits.quote: 2  Fill the hexagon
edits.fix: Delete the title; label 'Problem 2:'.

edits.quote: Fill a hexagon with blocks. Trace around each block. Then fill the next hexagon a new way!
edits.fix: Say what 'new' means (a different set of blocks, not the same blocks turned), e.g. 'Fill each hexagon with a different set of blocks.' Drop the exclamation.

edits.quote: Six 2-inch hexagon boards
edits.fix: Ten different block sets fill the hexagon (yellow; 2 reds; 3 blues; 6 greens; purple+blue; purple+2 greens; red+blue+green; red+3 greens; 2 blues+2 greens; blue+4 greens). Add boards (they fit four per row) so a quick child can keep going; this also helps the band's short volume.

edits.quote: One way: 2 reds (with picture)
edits.fix: Delete the worked example; it gives away one of the answers. The adult can model the first fill in the demonstration.

edits.quote: Talk about it. Did anyone use a purple block? Which way uses the most blocks? Which way uses the fewest?
edits.fix: Move to the adult notes, or make 'the fewest blocks / the most blocks' part of the problem.

edits.quote: 3  Fill the star
edits.fix: Delete the title; label 'Problem 3:'.

edits.quote: Star 1: use any blocks. ... How many blocks did you use?
edits.fix: With no goal, any count from 3 to 12 is correct and the child cannot tell when they are done. Ask for the fewest blocks. Also add the purple chevron to the block row: three purples fill the star exactly (6 is the best without purple).

edits.quote: Three blue-rhombus icons above Star 2
edits.fix: Show one blue icon. Three pictured blues suggest the star takes three, but it takes six.

edits.quote: Talk about it. How many points does a star have? Which blocks can fill a point? In Star 2, is there more than one way to use only blues?
edits.fix: Delete the filler point-counting question. The uniqueness question (answer: exactly one way, because each point forces its blue) is real: put it in the problem as 'Find every way to fill Star 2 with blues' or give it to the adult.

edits.quote: Your turn! Build a shape with blocks on the table. Trace around the outside on paper. Can a friend fill your shape with only blue blocks?
edits.fix: Remove the 'Your turn!' label and sidebar. Either make it a numbered problem with blank triangle-grid space to trace on, or move it to the adult notes.

edits.quote: 4  Big triangles
edits.fix: Delete the title; label 'Problem 4:'.

edits.quote: Then find the big green blocks. Which triangle does each one fit?
edits.fix: Name the 2x and 3x upscale greens and give a place to record the answer, e.g. 'How many big (2x) greens cover the largest triangle?' with a box. Right now there is nowhere to answer, and the callout's 'this triangle' is ambiguous.

edits.quote: Talk about it. Guess first, then count! Can you cover this triangle with the big green blocks?
edits.fix: 'Guess first' goes to the adult; fold the big-green task into the problem text (see previous edit) and delete the box.

edits.quote: 5  Only blue blocks?
edits.fix: Delete the title; label 'Problem 5:'.

edits.quote: Talk about it. Can anyone cover a big triangle with only blue blocks? Look at your three numbers. What do you notice?
edits.fix: Move to the adult notes. The pattern (fewest greens = 2, 3, 4 = side length) is the discovery, and the adult should prompt it.

edits.quote: Packet ends after P5 (about 28 minutes for a quick child)
edits.fix: About 10-15 minutes short. Add a substantial final problem in the same vein, e.g. fewest greens on a side-5 triangle and on a hexagon with corners removed, or 'make a shape blue blocks can fill and one they cannot', on full-size boards.

k-1.summary: Concrete, actual-size boards and a real entry to kernel 1 (P5 fewest greens, and P3 Star 2 with its forced unique tiling). But P1 is a trivial count of single-block outlines, Star 1 has no goal, and every page carries a 'Talk about it' box of adult commentary. The band also runs out roughly 10-15 minutes early for a quick child.

edits.quote: Board is actual size: each small triangle side is 1 inch. Print at 100%.   This bar is 1 inch: (all pages)
edits.fix: Replace with the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / PGQUG-23'; move the print check to the adult notes.

edits.quote: 1  Ups and downs
edits.fix: Delete the title; label 'Problem 1:'.
Delete the Name field.

edits.quote: 1. Put a dot in every UP [up] triangle on this board.
edits.fix: Delete this busywork sub-step (12 dots). Keep 'every small triangle points UP or DOWN' as the unnumbered shared rule for the activity.

edits.quote: Table: Block | covers [up] | covers [down], one row per block
edits.fix: The green (1/0 or 0/1) and red (2/1 or 1/2) give two answers depending on placement, but the table has one cell. Give room for every answer found, or ask directly which blocks always cover the same numbers.

edits.quote: Talk about it. Did any block give two different answers? Can you place a blue so that it covers two [up] triangles?
edits.fix: This is the point of the problem. Put the blue question in the problem text as the task, and delete the box.

edits.quote: 2  Possible or impossible?
edits.fix: Delete the title; label 'Problem 2:'.

edits.quote: Cover a board with blue rhombi only
edits.fix: 'Cover each board...'.

edits.quote: Then count the [up] and [down] triangles on the board. (plus [up]___ [down]___ blanks under A-D)
edits.fix: Delete the count instruction and the blanks. They print the method for the 'why impossible' question; leave the up/down count as an adult hint.

edits.quote: Talk about it. Every board has an even number of triangles. What do the impossible boards have in common? Why does that make them impossible?
edits.fix: This is the central question. Move it into the problem text (keep the even-number remark, which rules out the area argument) with a few lines to write on, and delete the box.

edits.quote: 3  Broken hexagons
edits.fix: Delete the title; label 'Problem 3:'.

edits.quote: Hexagon X / Hexagon Y (next to circled X / Y)
edits.fix: Delete the duplicate labels; the circled letters suffice.

edits.quote: [up] ___ [down] ___ blanks under X and Y
edits.fix: Delete; counting ups and downs is the idea children should find.

edits.quote: Make your own. Which two triangles could you take out of a whole hexagon so that it is still possible? So that it is impossible?
edits.fix: Good task, but it has a label, sits in a box, and gives no boards. Make it part of the problem text and print two compact side-2 hexagon grids to shade the holes on.

edits.quote: 4  Fewest gaps
edits.fix: Delete the title; label 'Problem 4:'.

edits.quote: put in as many blues as you can, then fill the gaps with greens. Try to use as few greens as possible!
edits.fix: 'As many blues' and 'as few greens' are the same goal. Keep one: 'Fill the gaps with greens, using as few greens as possible.'

edits.quote: Your best so far. (Board A on page 2 is the side-2 triangle.) + table Side 2/3/4 | most blues | fewest greens
edits.fix: Delete. The same rows are repeated in the P5 table; record once there.

edits.quote: Talk about it. Compare with your group. Can anyone beat your number of greens? Look at the triangles your greens are sitting on. Are they [up] or [down]?
edits.fix: Move to the adult notes; the last two sentences hand over the key observation.

edits.quote: A plan that always works? Describe a way to place the blues that leaves only as many gaps as the side length. Would your plan work for every big triangle?
edits.fix: Drop the label. Do not state the answer (gaps = side length) before children find it in the P5 table. Rewrite: 'Find a way of placing blues that works on every big triangle. How many greens does it leave?' and place it after the table.

edits.quote: 5  Bigger and bigger
edits.fix: Delete the title; label 'Problem 5:'.

edits.quote: Side 5. Use as many blues as you can. Fill the gaps with greens.
edits.fix: The rule was already given in P4. Keep only the instruction to do the side-5 board.

edits.quote: Purple puzzle. Would purple pieces help you leave fewer gaps? Try covering a purple with blues.
edits.fix: Drop the label and the second sentence, which gives the reason away. Put the question in the problem text: 'Could purple chevrons with blues leave fewer gaps than blues alone? Explain.'

edits.quote: (Hint: each blue covers one [up] and one [down].)
edits.fix: Delete the hint; it is the whole proof. The adult can give it if needed.

grades-2-3.summary: A well-chosen kernel-1 sequence with correct boards: A and C impossible, B and D possible; hexagon X impossible (two up-holes) and Y tileable (4 ways); fewest greens equals the side length. The child's discovery is spoiled repeatedly by count-the-ups instructions, hint boxes, a printed 'as many gaps as the side length' and a closing hint. Headings, labels, Talk-about-it boxes and a duplicated table need cutting.

edits.quote: Hexagon board is actual size... / Big board is actual size... This bar is 1 inch: (pages 3 and 4 have no footer at all)
edits.fix: Put the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / PGQUG-45' on every page, pages 3 and 4 included; move the print check to the adult notes.

edits.quote: 1  Three blues, two ways
edits.fix: Delete the title; label 'Problem 1:'.
Delete the Name field.

edits.quote: Today we only use blue rhombi.
edits.fix: Make it a plain shared rule: 'Use only blue rhombi.'

edits.quote: 1. Cover this hexagon with 3 blues. There are exactly two ways. Build both. 2. Lift the three blues and turn them... This move is called a flip. (both tilings then drawn directly below)
edits.fix: This is a two-minute demonstration with its answer printed underneath, not a grade 4-5 problem. Make the three directions and the flip picture the unnumbered shared rules, and start the numbered problems with the tall hexagon. Move the 3D question to where it has work to do (see P5).

edits.quote: 3. Look in 3D. ... Stare at them. What do you see?
edits.fix: Drop the 'Look in 3D.' label and 'Stare at them.'

edits.quote: Coming up. Bigger hexagons have many tilings. You will hunt for all of them, connect them by flips, and find a secret code hiding inside every tiling.
edits.fix: Delete the narration.

edits.quote: 2  The tall hexagon
edits.fix: Delete the title; label 'Problem 2:'.

edits.quote: Tips. • One person builds, one checks that it is new, one draws. • Stuck? Look for three blues that make a small hexagon, and flip them!
edits.fix: Move both to the adult notes; one is group management and the other is a hint.

edits.quote: Draw each new one in a box below and give it a letter.
edits.fix: The boxes are already lettered A-H; delete 'and give it a letter'.

edits.quote: Eight drawing boxes A-H (and the eight-column Tiling A-H / Word table on p.4)
edits.fix: The tall hexagon has 6 tilings. Lettered slots for 8 suggest two are missing. Leave the spare boxes unlettered and give the table six columns plus spares.

edits.quote: 3  Flips
edits.fix: Delete the title; label 'Problem 3:'.

edits.quote: Wherever three blues make a small hexagon (shaded yellow), you can flip them.
edits.fix: Repeats the flip definition from p.1. State the flip once in the shared rules; keep the 'neighbors' definition here.

edits.quote: Move letters around until your map looks tidy.
edits.fix: Pencil letters cannot be moved. Say 'Draw it on a whiteboard first, then copy a tidy version here.'

edits.quote: Sub-numbered parts with bold labels: '1. Flip map.', '3. Round trips.', '3. Challenge.', '4. Look in 3D.'
edits.fix: Each part is a substantial task. Number them as 'Problem N:' and drop the bold labels.

edits.quote: 4  Ribbons: a secret code
edits.fix: Delete the cutesy title; label 'Problem N:'.

edits.quote: 2. List every word made of two L's and two R's. Does each word give a tiling? So how many tilings does the tall hexagon have?
edits.fix: This walks the child through the counting argument. Rewrite as one open question: 'Which words can a ribbon spell? Use ribbons to prove your list on page 2 has every tiling.'

edits.quote: 4. The L-score of a word is the sum of the places where the L's are. For L R R L it is 1 + 4 = 5. What does one flip do to the L-score? Use this to explain why a round trip can never have an odd number of flips.
edits.fix: The invariant is handed over, and 'never' answers P3's round-trip question. Keep 'Explain why no round trip has an odd number of flips' and give the L-score to the adult as a hint.

edits.quote: 5  The big hexagon
edits.fix: Delete the title; label 'Problem N:'.

edits.quote: (Your flip map from page 3 can help!)
edits.fix: Delete the hint. Pairs fit together exactly when the left word is below the right word in the flip order; the adult can point this out.

edits.quote: 3. Challenge. ... Keep track on paper or a whiteboard.
edits.fix: Drop the 'Challenge.' label and the filler sentence. Keep 'How many tilings does the big hexagon have? Explain how you counted.' (answer 20).

edits.quote: 4. Look in 3D. Shade one of your tilings like the picture. What do you see? What does a flip do to it?
edits.fix: Near-verbatim repeat of p.1 and vague. Give it a task: 'Each tiling is a stack of cubes in a 2x2x2 corner. How many cubes are in your stack? What does one flip do to the number of cubes?' This links to the parity question.

grades-4-5.summary: The strongest band: it develops kernel 2 through a good sequence. The tall hexagon has 6 tilings and X to Y takes 4 flips; ribbons give a bijection with LLRR-type words; round-trip parity follows; the 2x2x2 hexagon has 20 tilings. All diagrams and example ribbons check out. Edits are mostly about voice and over-guidance: a trivial demo page as P1, narration and tips boxes, and the counting argument and the L-score invariant handed to the child.

overall.strongest: Grades 4-5 is mathematically deep and correct, and it carries kernel 2 (flips, ribbons, parity, counting the 20 tilings) through a real sequence on actual-size boards.
overall.weakest: K-1 opens with a trivial count of single-block outlines, gives Star 1 no goal and runs out 10-15 minutes early, and all three bands share the same machine-written frame (titles, Name field, Talk-about-it boxes, nonstandard footer) that has to be stripped.
